finding.statement: The shape as first specified needed eight corrections, in descending order of how much each changes a score. Margaret belongs on the mother axis as a substantial soft hit. The Mary attribute has a primary bound and the Richard and John attributes do not - Mary Gurney married Daniel Shed at Braintree in 1647, so at a minimum marriage age of sixteen she was born by 1631, while Richard about 1630 and John about 1633 rest entirely on compiled estimates with no primary record behind them; this matters directly, because Hitcham's Mary of January 1630/1 satisfies the primary bound exactly while looking three years off the traditional date. The two marriage attributes are mutually exclusive, so scoring both double-counts one marriage. The paternal-grandfather attribute is a derived prediction rather than an independent observation, conditional on Richard being the eldest son, so a hit on it is a hit on a hypothesis and a miss is weak evidence. A departure attribute should be added - the household's records stop between 1635 and 1641 with no burial or probate for the head - but only with its coverage control attached, since two false departure gaps have already been produced by omitting it, and on a properly controlled test only Ackworth currently passes. A penalty is needed for children with no colonial counterpart, since as specified the shape can only reward matches and never penalise surplus. The surname attribute is a weighted scale rather than a single tick. And Peter, Isaac and Sarah must be excluded from scoring rather than treated as missing children, because their absence from English registers is expected. A ninth rule arrived from the elimination side: three undated role-row households, one of them earlier described as the single most important loose end in the work, were dated on a second instrument and resolved to 1687, 1704 and 1710 - so an undated role row is not evidence of an in-window household until it is dated elsewhere.

finding.statement: Forename variants are a weighted scale in exactly the way surname variants are, and Margaret belongs on the mother axis as a substantial soft hit rather than as a different name. In seventeenth-century hands the letters g and y carry near-identical looping descenders, and Margaret was routinely contracted by clerks to Marg. or Mgt. to save paper and ink - so the single letter distinguishing the written token from Mary is precisely the letter most likely to be ambiguous. A Marg. written with a looping g reads as Mary to a later clerk, a nineteenth-century transcriber or a modern indexer, and a Mary is equally extendable to Margaret: the corruption is introduced by the transcription chain and runs in both directions. The corpus supplies a worked example - Tittleshall with Godwick, Norfolk, 1620 returns the same child twice, father Henry in both rows, with the mother indexed Anne in one transcript and Mary in the other. The adopted weighting gives full weight to Mary, Marie, Marye, Maria, Marya and Mria; substantial soft-hit weight to Marg, Marg., Mgt, Margaret, Margarett and Margret; partial weight to Margery and Margerie; and excludes Molly and Polly as eighteenth-century hypocorisms that cannot appear in a 1620s register. The same logic governs the father axis, where Jone and Joan in a father field are treated as a contracted or Latin Johannes rather than as a woman - the county sets demonstrably do both, indexing the father of Joseph Garnam at Norwich St Giles in 1618 as Jone and the father of Gregorye Gurnall at King's Lynn in 1615 as Katheryne.

negativeResult.collection: FreeREG parish transcriptions; eight FindMyPast county baptism sets; FindMyPast cross-collection parent search (sid=102)
limitations: FreeREG's surname matching is exact and non-soundex, so its arm depends entirely on the twenty spellings actually queried.
The national parent pool does not reach every county set, which is why the county-set sweep is paired with it.
The county sweep covers eight counties only - Norfolk, Essex, Northamptonshire, Oxfordshire, Cambridgeshire, Middlesex, Westminster and Berkshire - so this is not an England-wide county-set negative.
The national parent search's variant engine is loose, so its eight Margaret rows are fuzzy-match noise rather than Gurney households; the negative rests on reading them, not on the count.

finding.statement: Admitting Margaret to the mother axis changed no candidate score, because the axis was then searched and it is empty. Across FreeREG's 585 captured rows, five households carry a Margaret-family mother - Norwich 1638, Bardwell in Suffolk 1643 and 1645, and Mamble and Bayton in Worcestershire 1637 - and none has a father in the John family. Across 705 rows from eight FindMyPast county baptism sets, seven rows carry a Margaret-family mother, to fathers Robert, Edward, Michael and William, and none has a father in the John family at any date. The national cross-collection parent search bounded 1610-1650 returns eight rows for a father John with a mother Margaret, not one of them a genuine Gurney - the surname column reading '?', 'Fosse', 'G...Ds' and 'G?', fuzzy-match noise from Cornwall, Cheshire and Scotland. The negative is interpretable because the identical query shape with mother Mary returns the known Eythorne household and the Westminster Gurley household: the instrument was working when it returned nothing for Margaret.
